title: Sobornost
hookLine: Khomiakov: the church as free unity in love

lines: IT SEEMED GOOD TO THE SPIRIT, AND TO US.
cards: A tense meeting in Jerusalem. Followers of Jesus who aren't Jewish are joining, and believers disagree about what to ask of them. Paul and Barnabas have already argued it out in Antioch.
So the apostles and elders gather. Peter speaks. The whole room goes quiet and listens to Barnabas and Paul.
James speaks. At last they send out a letter with an unusual line in it: "For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us." Not one voice ruling.
Not the loudest side winning. A Russian thinker named Alexei Khomiakov built his whole picture of the church around that kind of togetherness.

teach.h: A WORD WITH NO ENGLISH MATCH
teach.b: Sobornost is a Russian word with no neat English match. Translators try conciliarity, or togetherness, or catholicity in its old sense of wholeness.
Tradition ties it to sobor, a word for a gathering, a council, or a cathedral. Khomiakov used it for the church as a free unity in love. Hold both halves.
Unity: the church isn't a pile of separate believers who happen to share a building.
It's one life, like the believers in Acts, who "were of one heart and of one soul."
Freely: that unity can't be forced, not by a ruler, not by fear, not by pressure.
The truth, Khomiakov said, isn't kept by any one person alone, but by the whole church together, bound in love, and love keeps the knowing safe.
He set this against two shortcuts he saw in the Western churches: Rome, to him, held unity without enough freedom, and Protestants kept freedom without enough unity.
Catholic and Protestant Christians describe their own churches differently, and wouldn't accept that picture of them; Orthodox writers since have debated it too.
But they still use the word for something hard: being many and one at once. Set it beside Kierkegaard's crowd, where nobody answers for anything.
Sobornost isn't a crowd at all: a body where every person answers freely, and still they answer together.

how: Orthodox Christians often speak of the church's life as conciliar: bishops meet in councils, and the faith is understood to be held by the whole people of God together, not by any one person alone.

games.q: you're at the Jerusalem meeting in Acts 15. the believers are divided. how does the matter get settled?
o: one apostle rules, and everyone obeys.
everyone goes home and decides alone.
they gather, listen, and write: it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us.
games.why: they talk, they listen, Peter, Paul, Barnabas and James all speak, and the letter names the Spirit and the church together.

practice: Think of one small choice you share with someone: what's for dinner, a weekend plan, how to split a chore.

Picture a third way between deciding for them and going along to keep the peace: you each say what you hope for, you listen, and you look for what seems good to both of you. If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer by name.

wordCard.voice: Sobornost. The Russian word Khomiakov used for the church as a free unity in love: many people, one life, and no force.

orig.note: Russian: togetherness, conciliarity — the church as many people sharing one free life.

carryVoice: Your line: together, freely. A unity that nobody forces on anyone. Rest well.
